title: Streaming dropout surge thresholds and graceful-degradation playbook
creator: Asha Menon
description:
Summary:
During a capacity surge on 2026-03-08 we observed elevated streaming dropout rates across multiple hosted regions. Symptoms included abrupt websocket disconnects mid-response, truncated token sequences (partial tokens delivered to clients), and incorrect client-side retry behavior that led to duplicate message fragments. The outage was correlated with a short-lived spike in inference concurrency and a simultaneous change in batching heuristics deployed in runtime-1.21 that increased per-request memory pressure for long-context sessions.

Why this matters:
Streaming stability is a top-level SLO for customers using live generation for UXs (chat, co-writing, real-time assistants). Truncated or duplicated token streams compromise UX and can surface as corrupted outputs, leading to user-facing errors and support escalations.

RCA (concise):
- A recent batching tweak increased in-flight KV-cache allocations for active sessions with >2048 tokens, increasing per-worker memory usage by ~15%.
- Autoscaler reacted to CPU indicators but did not account for rapid GPU memory pressure spikes; some pods hit OOMprotection/eviction windows causing abrupt socket closure without proper token-commit flush.
- Backpressure signals originating in runtime (per-session queue depth) were throttled by an older rate limiter, delaying shedding decisions until drop thresholds were exceeded.
- Client reconnection semantics lacked a deterministic token-commit checkpoint; clients reconnected and replayed prefixes, causing duplicated tokens for a subset of sessions.

Proposed scope for this ticket (deliverables):
1) Implement a surge-threshold policy for streaming that proactively enters graceful-degradation mode when aggregated per-node streaming memory exceeds 70% for >10s. Graceful-degradation modes include: reduce max-active-sessions, tighten per-session concurrency, and switch to short-polling fallback for long-context sessions.
2) Add an explicit in-protocol token-commit checkpoint message sent to clients at stable boundaries (every N complete tokens or at generation segment boundaries) to avoid ambiguous partial-token state on reconnect.
3) Surface new metrics and alerts: per-node streaming_memory_pct, streaming_active_sessions_skew, token_fragment_rate, and client-reconnect-loop-count. Create SLO burn dashboards and PagerDuty alert thresholds.
4) Autoscaler change: add GPU memory pressure as a first-class scaling signal and fast-path eviction mitigation to avoid abrupt socket termination.
5) Short-term mitigations: revert the batching tweak for long-context sessions on runtime-1.21; deploy a Canary of the graceful-degradation policy in us-east-1 for 48 hours.

Acceptance criteria:
- Graceful-degradation policy implemented and unit tested, with feature flag gating and runtime config knobs.
- Token-commit checkpoint implemented in protocol v2 and documented in API changelog.
- New metrics emitted (Prometheus) and dashboards in Console showing meaningful baselines.
- Canary run for 48 hours with no increase in dropout rate over baseline; rollout plan for global release.

Notes on trade-offs and constraints:
- Aggressive early shedding reduces customer throughput; policy must be tuned to avoid false positives. Initial threshold is conservative (70% for 10s) but can be tuned after Canary.
- Token-commit checkpoints introduce small protocol overhead and slight latency for checkpoint acknowledgements; we will batch checkpoints (every 16 tokens or at segment boundary) to amortize cost.
- Short-poll fallback increases per-request load on control-plane but saves worker memory; we must monitor control-plane load during Canary.

Deliverable owners and rough timelines:
- Runtime changes (surge policy, token-commit): Liam OConnor (owner) + Runtime team — 2 weeks to implement + 1 week of integration testing.
- Autoscaler changes: Priya Shah (SRE) — 1 week to add GPU mem signal + 1 week to test scaling behavior.
- Telemetry + Dashboards: Miguel Alvarez (Observability) — 4 days.
- Client SDK changes (ack handling): Ember Li (SDK) — 1 week to add reconnect-safe client logic and tests.

Links and artifacts:
- Incident timeline and raw logs: https://drive.redwood.ai/incidents/2026-03-streaming-surge
- Heap/alloc histogram and flame graphs: https://dashboards.redwood.ai/d/heap/streaming-allocs
- Initial PR (proposed slow-shed design): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/5128
- Runbook proposal draft: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/Runtime/Streaming+Graceful+Degradation+Playbook

Longer-term follow-ups (out of scope for this ticket but tracked):
- Rework batching heuristics to account for long-context memory cost explicitly.
- End-to-end integration tests that simulate GPU memory-pressure and verify safe reconnect semantics.
- Expand token-commit protocol to support resumable continuation tokens for long-running sessions.

2026-03-13 - Implementation update: Token-commit message format drafted; PR scaffold created (https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/5128). Liam started runtime module for surge detector. Added unit tests for state transitions.
